Approaching the Thermodynamic Limit with Neural-Network Quantum States

Luciano Loris Viteritti Thanks: These authors contributed equally. Correspondence should be addressed to rrende@flatironinstitute.org and luciano.viteritti@epfl.ch Affiliation: Institute of Physics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland    Riccardo Rende Thanks: These authors contributed equally. Correspondence should be addressed to rrende@flatironinstitute.org and luciano.viteritti@epfl.ch Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, 162 5th Avenue, New York, NY 10010    Subir Sachdev Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, 162 5th Avenue, New York, NY 10010 Affiliation: Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge MA 02138, USA    Giuseppe Carleo Affiliation: Institute of Physics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Accessing the thermodynamic-limit properties of strongly correlated quantum matter requires simulations on very large lattices, a regime that remains challenging for numerical methods, especially in frustrated two-dimensional systems. We introduce the Spatial Attention mechanism, a minimal and physically interpretable inductive bias for Neural-Network Quantum States, implemented as a single learned length scale within the Transformer architecture. This bias stabilizes large-scale optimization and enables access to thermodynamic-limit physics through highly accurate simulations on unprecedented system sizes within the Variational Monte Carlo framework. Applied to the spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} triangular-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet, our approach achieves state-of-the-art results on clusters of up to 42×4242\times 42 sites. The ability to simulate such large systems allows controlled finite-size scaling of energies and order parameters, enabling the extraction of experimentally relevant quantities such as spin-wave velocities and uniform susceptibilities. In turn, we find extrapolated thermodynamic limit energies systematically better than those obtained with tensor-network approaches such as iPEPS. The resulting magnetization is strongly renormalized, ℳ0=0.148​(1)\mathcal{M}_{0}=0.148(1) (about 30%30\% of the classical value), revealing that less accurate variational states systematically overestimate magnetic order. Analysis of the optimized wave function further suggests an intrinsically non-local sign structure, indicating that the sign problem cannot be removed by local basis transformations. We finally demonstrate the generality of the method by obtaining state-of-the-art energies for a J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model on a 20×2020\times 20 square lattice, outperforming Residual Convolutional Neural Networks.

I Introduction

Extracting thermodynamic-limit properties of strongly correlated quantum systems is a central goal in condensed matter physics [1, 72]: reaching sufficiently large lattices is essential for performing controlled finite-size scaling and reliably extracting thermodynamic-limit quantities such as order parameters, excitation gaps, or correlation lengths [57, 75]. Despite major progress over the past decades, existing numerical methods struggle to balance accuracy and scalability, especially for frustrated systems in two dimensions, where sign problems or entanglement constraints make large-scale calculations prohibitive [90, 3, 20, 80].

Among the many approaches developed to tackle this problem, Neural-Network Quantum States (NQS) [9, 41] have emerged as a particularly promising class of variational Ansätze [10, 95, 96, 71]. By leveraging the expressive power of modern deep-learning architectures, NQS can efficiently represent highly entangled quantum states [42, 81, 23] and capture complicated sign structures that are inaccessible to conventional methods [88, 94, 66, 10].

As in broader machine learning, the success of NQS relies on inductive biases [52, 19]: architectural priors that guide learning toward physically relevant solutions using finite data and noisy gradients. This naturally raises the question: which inductive biases are most relevant for variational descriptions of ground states? Physical Hamiltonians typically involve local interactions, which constrain how correlations decay and how information propagates [46]. This behavior is formalized by the cluster property: correlations between operators vanish as their separation, either in space or in time, increases [31]. Importantly, the locality of the Hamiltonian does not imply short-ranged correlations in the corresponding ground states: gapless phases and critical points display algebraic correlations and long-range entanglement. This distinction is crucial for designing a proper variational state. A locality-inspired bias can therefore be valuable as an optimization prior without imposing hard representational constraints such as finite correlation length or area-law truncation.

Here, we propose an inductive bias for Transformer-based NQS inspired by the cluster property. This bias is realized through the Spatial Attention mechanism, a minimal and physically motivated modification of the attention mechanism [95, 96, 85], in which attention weights are reweighted by an explicit distance-dependent kernel controlled by a single length-scale parameter (see Section II). Variants of the attention mechanism that explicitly encode spatial or distance-dependent biases have been previously proposed and successfully applied in different machine-learning settings [101, 86, 107]. Crucially, the inductive bias we propose is Hamiltonian-agnostic: it encodes only a universal geometric bias rather than model-specific information. Empirically, we find that this single ingredient stabilizes optimization on large two-dimensional lattices, starting from random initialization and without providing prior information about the sign structure [45], enabling accurate calculations on frustrated systems containing thousands of spins, an ability that has remained out of reach for existing NQS architectures.

To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we apply it to the spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice, a paradigmatic example of a frustrated magnet, where geometric constraints prevent the use of sign-problem-free Quantum Monte Carlo methods [74, 75, 4]. Although there is consensus that the ground state exhibits 120∘120^{\circ} Néel magnetic order, quantitative estimates of the magnetization vary widely 0.16≲ℳ0≲0.280.16\lesssim\mathcal{M}_{0}\lesssim 0.28 [25, 40, 34, 24, 28, 8, 100, 43, 68, 108, 21, 106, 44, 36, 54, 30, 56, 44] (see Table 2). This dispersion reflects the difficulty of combining high variational accuracy with controlled finite-size scaling at large system sizes. Our method overcomes this barrier: we reach cluster sizes up to 42×4242\times 42, obtaining state-of-the-art variational energies and finding the lowest thermodynamic-limit magnetization reported to date, ℳ0=0.148​(1)\mathcal{M}_{0}=0.148(1), about 30%30\% of the classical value, highlighting the role of strong quantum fluctuations. Moreover, we show that less accurate variational approximations systematically overestimate the magnetization, providing a concrete explanation for part of the spread in previous results. From finite-size scaling of energy and magnetization, we extract the velocity of low-energy spin excitations and susceptibilities [48, 103, 78] and compare it with linear spin wave theory [14, 12, 91] and the Schwinger boson approach [24].

Large-scale access also enables a systematic analysis of the ground-state sign structure, a central question in frustrated systems. Using the optimized variational states, we explicitly test candidate sign rules proposed for this model [37], finding that the sign overlap decreases exponentially with system size. This indicates that even extended local sign rules rapidly fail to reproduce the exact structure. While this does not constitute a no-go theorem against all possible local basis transformations, it provides quantitative evidence that the sign structure is highly non-local and supports the idea that the Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the triangular lattice has an intrinsic sign problem.

Finally, to demonstrate that our approach is not limited to a particular model, we study the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model [35, 58] on a 20×2020\times 20 square lattice, achieving state-of-the-art results in comparison to all the other existing variational methods [10].

Taken together, these results show that embedding a minimal, physically motivated inductive bias into Transformer-NQS can dramatically improve optimization stability and scalability, thereby enabling controlled access to the thermodynamic limit in frustrated two-dimensional quantum magnets.

II Spatial Attention mechanism

Variational approaches based on NQS represent the many-body wave function by mapping spin configurations 𝝈=(σ1,…,σN)\boldsymbol{\sigma}=(\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{N}), with σi=±1\sigma_{i}=\pm 1, to complex amplitudes Ψθ​(𝝈)\Psi_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) parametrized by a neural network with parameters θ\theta. Expectation values are computed using Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) [4], and the parameters θ\theta are optimized via Stochastic Reconfiguration (SR) [84, 4, 66, 10]. Among the architectures proposed for frustrated quantum magnets, the Vision Transformer (ViT) wave function [95, 64, 96, 60, 67, 97, 11] has demonstrated high accuracy in two dimensions.

The core component of the Transformer architecture is the attention mechanism [92], which processes a sequence of nn input vectors (𝐱1,…,𝐱n)(\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{n}), with 𝐱i∈ℝd\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and produces an output sequence of equal length (𝐀1,…,𝐀n)(\mathbf{A}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{A}_{n}), referred to as attention vectors, with 𝐀i∈ℝd\mathbf{A}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. A detailed description of how the input vectors 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i} are constructed from a spin configuration 𝝈\boldsymbol{\sigma} is provided in Sec. V.2.

In this work, we introduce the Spatial Attention mechanism that softly biases the attention weights via a distance-dependent kernel. The resulting attention vectors are given by

Ai=∑j=1ne−γ​d​(i,j)∑j′=1ne−γ​d​(i,j′)​αi​j​V​xj,\textbf{A}_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{e^{-\gamma d(i,j)}}{\sum_{j^{\prime}=1}^{n}e^{-\gamma d(i,j^{\prime})}}\alpha_{ij}V\textbf{x}_{j}\ , (1)

where the attention coefficients αi​j\alpha_{ij} and value matrix VV are trainable parameters. The key modification compared to previous attention mechanisms [95, 96, 62, 63] is the multiplicative factor depending on the distance d⁡(i,j)d(i,j), defined as the Euclidean distance between lattice sites ii and jj, and the inverse length scale γ>0\gamma>0, which is learned during optimization and controls the characteristic spatial range of correlations.

Although optimized Transformer wave functions typically exhibit an effective attenuation of attention weights with increasing spatial separation [65, 96, 29, 63], learning this distance dependence from random initialization becomes progressively more challenging as the system size increases. By explicitly encoding this physically motivated structure, the Spatial Attention mechanism substantially enhances optimization stability in the large-system regime.

Crucially, the proposed modification constitutes a soft and learnable geometric prior that preserves global connectivity, and the architecture continuously reduces to standard attention when the inverse length scales vanish. More flexibility is introduced with the adoption of the Multi-Head Attention mechanism [92], where each head is associated with an independent length-scale parameter, allowing the Ansatz to represent multiple correlation scales simultaneously [29]. By employing deep architectures, successive layers can further refine the effective correlation lengths. Refer to Fig. 1 for a graphical representation of the mechanism.

Operationally, Eq. 1 constitutes a simple modification of the standard Attention mechanism and can be implemented as a one-line change in the ViT architecture 11 1 See the NetKet tutorial [https://netket.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/ViT-wave-function.html..

III Heisenberg Triangular lattice

As a concrete and physically relevant application of our approach, we investigate the ground state properties of the spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} Heisenberg Hamiltonian on the triangular lattice

H^=J​∑⟨i,j⟩𝑺^i⋅𝑺^j,\hat{H}=J\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{j}\ , (2)

where 𝑺^i=(Six,Siy,Siz)\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{i}=(S_{i}^{x},S_{i}^{y},S_{i}^{z}) is the spin-1/21/2 operator at site ii, and J>0J>0 is the antiferromagnetic coupling among nearest-neighbors. All calculations are performed on periodic L×LL\times L clusters with LL chosen as a multiple of 33, ensuring commensurability with the three-sublattice 120∘120^{\circ} Néel order [8, 99].

III.1 Energy and Magnetization

To assess the quantitative performance of the spatial-attention–based ViT wave function, we first benchmark it against leading variational Ansätze. As summarized in Table 1, the ViT achieves significantly lower energies than Gutzwiller-projected states [105, 26] and recent neural-network wave functions based on Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) [55] across all accessible system sizes. Notably, on the largest cluster studied (42×4242\times 42) the variational energy is below the best previously reported value for the 18×1818\times 18 cluster. Overall, the ViT improves the relative energy accuracy by more than an order of magnitude compared to other approaches.

We next exploit the large accessible sizes to perform controlled finite-size scaling of the energy. For a two dimensional antiferromagnet, the leading correction to the thermodynamic-limit energy is expected to scale as 1/L31/L^{3} [22, 73, 14, 76] (refer to Section III.3 and Supplementary Information for additional details). As shown in Fig. 2a, the numerical data of the variational energy per site follow a linear scaling in 1/L31/L^{3} for L≥24L\geq 24 (purple triangles), allowing for a reliable extrapolation to L→+∞L\to+\infty. We compare our extrapolated results with the most accurate tensor-network estimates obtained from iPEPS calculations performed directly in the thermodynamic limit at finite bond dimension DD (black horizontal dashed lines) [30, 56]. Remarkably, our results are below the iPEPS estimations up to L=42L=42 and reach state-of-the-art results in the thermodynamic limit. Moreover, for each system size, we perform an energy-variance extrapolation (see Section V.3) and compare the extrapolated energies (red rhombi) with the iPEPS extrapolations obtained in the limit D→+∞D\rightarrow+\infty (red horizontal dashed lines). From this analysis, we estimate a thermodynamic-limit energy per site of -0.55168(2), which is lower than the corresponding iPEPS estimates.

In Fig. 2b we report estimations of the accuracy of the variational state. In the upper panel we show the relative energy error as a function of the system size for three levels of symmetry restoration (none, translations only, full point-group C6​vC_{6v}), computed with respect to the corresponding zero-variance extrapolations (see Section V.3). In the lower panel of the same figure, we also present the V-score [102], a reference-free accuracy metric for variational methods. Both measures remain essentially stable as the system size grows. Importantly, this is achieved with an approximately fixed parameter count, P≈4.5×105P\approx 4.5\times 10^{5}, for all LL (see Section V.2), indicating that accuracy does not rely on scaling the network with the lattice size. Size consistency is a key requirement for a scalable variational Ansatz, and in practice, many variational states achieve high accuracy on small lattices but exhibit a systematic degradation in performance as the cluster size grows [94].

Let us now move to the study of the magnetic properties, assessed through the static spin structure factor C⁡(𝒒)=∑𝑹ei​𝒒⋅𝑹​⟨𝑺^𝟎⋅𝑺^𝑹⟩{C(\boldsymbol{q})=\sum_{\boldsymbol{R}}e^{i\boldsymbol{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{R}}\langle\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{\boldsymbol{0}}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{\boldsymbol{R}}\rangle}, where the expectation value is evaluated over the variational state. For a periodic cluster L×LL\times L, the order parameter of the 120∘120^{\circ} Néel order is detected by ℳ2​(L)=C⁡(𝑸)/L2{\mathcal{M}^{2}(L)=C(\boldsymbol{Q})/L^{2}} with 𝑸=(4​π/3,0){\boldsymbol{Q}=(4\pi/3,0)} [33, 54]. In Fig. 3a we show the order parameter ℳ⁡(L)\mathcal{M}(L) versus 1/L1/L and its extrapolation to the thermodynamic limit. Our data yield a thermodynamic-limit magnetization ℳ0=0.148​(1)\mathcal{M}_{0}=0.148(1), the smallest among all the available estimates (see Table 2 for a collection of previous calculations). In particular, we emphasize that the magnetization predicted by linear spin-wave theory (SW) is 0.239 [14, 12, 91], exhibiting a relative error of approximately 62%62\% with respect to the fully quantum result. This differs significantly from the square-lattice Heisenberg model, where SW predicts the magnetization with an error of only about 1%1\% [38, 73]. This comparison suggests that, despite the presence of magnetic order in the triangular-lattice Heisenberg model, achieving a quantitatively accurate fully quantum description remains highly nontrivial. To clarify why magnetization estimates can vary widely across methods (refer to Table 2), in Fig. 3b we track the order parameter during the optimization procedure for L=30L=30. As the energy decreases and the wave function becomes more accurate, the magnetization monotonically reduces [96]. This directly indicates that limited variational accuracy can lead to a systematic overestimate of magnetic order and highlights the importance of high-precision wave-function optimization in frustrated systems.

III.2 Finite-Size Scaling

Tensor-network methods such as iPEPS operate directly in the thermodynamic limit and have achieved remarkable success in describing ground-state energies and local observables [98, 17, 18, 39, 93, 30, 56]. At the same time, working exclusively in the infinite-system setting comes with intrinsic limitations: quantities that rely on finite-size scaling cannot be accessed. By contrast, accurate variational wave functions defined on large periodic lattices allow for controlled finite-size scaling analyses of both the energy and order parameters, providing direct access to physically relevant properties. In the case of the antiferromagnetic triangular lattice, analytic expressions for the leading finite-size corrections can be derived and used to quantitatively fit the numerical data.

At low energy and long distances, the spin fluctuations on the triangular lattice can be captured by the parameterization

𝑺i​(τ)=ℳ0​[𝒏1​(𝒙i,τ)​cos⁡(𝑸⋅𝒙i)+𝒏2​(𝒙i,τ)​sin⁡(𝑸⋅𝒙i)],{\boldsymbol{S}}_{i}(\tau)=\mathcal{M}_{0}\left[{\boldsymbol{n}}_{1}({\boldsymbol{x}}_{i},\tau)\cos({\boldsymbol{Q}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{x}}_{i})+{\boldsymbol{n}}_{2}({\boldsymbol{x}}_{i},\tau)\sin({\boldsymbol{Q}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{x}}_{i})\right]\ , (3)

where ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} is the ground state ordered moment in the infinite lattice, 𝑸=(4​π/3,0){\boldsymbol{Q}}=(4\pi/3,0) is the ordering wavevector, and 𝒏1,𝒏2{\boldsymbol{n}}_{1},{\boldsymbol{n}}_{2} are slowly varying functions of space (𝒙{\boldsymbol{x}}) and imaginary time (τ\tau) obeying the constraints |𝒏|12=|𝒏2|2=1|{\boldsymbol{n}}|_{1}^{2}=|{\boldsymbol{n}}_{2}|^{2}=1, 𝒏1⋅𝒏2=0{\boldsymbol{n}}_{1}\cdot{\boldsymbol{n}}_{2}=0. From the symmetry of the ordered state, we obtain the low energy description as a non-linear σ\sigma-model [16, 15]

𝒮=∫d2​x​𝑑τ​∑μ=𝒙,τ1gμ​[∂μz†​∂μz−γμ4​(z†​∂μz−∂μz†​z)2].{\cal S}=\int d^{2}xd\tau\,\sum_{\mu={\boldsymbol{x}},\tau}\frac{1}{g_{\mu}}\left[\partial_{\mu}z^{\dagger}\partial_{\mu}z-\frac{\gamma_{\mu}}{4}\left(z^{\dagger}\partial_{\mu}z-\partial_{\mu}z^{\dagger}z\right)^{2}\right]\ . (4)

Together with the strong renormalization of the magnetization ℳ0\mathcal{M}_{0} (refer to Section III.1 and Table 2), this highlights that a quantitatively reliable description of the triangular-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet requires the inclusion of strong quantum effects that are not captured by SW contrary to the square lattice case. Importantly, spin-wave velocities and susceptibilities are experimentally accessible quantities, and the values reported here therefore provide a stringent benchmark for candidate materials realizing the triangular-lattice Heisenberg model [87, 103, 78, 79].

III.3 Non-Local Sign Structure

Beyond energies and order parameters, frustrated magnets raise a fundamental question about the structure of the ground state: is the sign problem a removable basis artefact, or does it reflect a genuinely non-local sign structure? For the pure Heisenberg model on bipartite lattices, the Marshall-Peierls sign rule provides a local basis transformation that renders the ground state non-negative in the computational basis [49]. No analogous prescription is known for the triangular lattice.

A notable attempt in this direction was proposed by Huse and Elser [37], who introduced an extended sign construction combining the classical three-sublattice phase factor

Tclass​(𝝈)=exp⁡[i​2​π6​(∑i∈Bσiz−∑i∈Cσiz)],{T_{\text{class}}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})=\exp\!\left[i\frac{2\pi}{6}\left(\sum_{i\in\mathrm{B}}\sigma_{i}^{z}-\sum_{i\in\mathrm{C}}\sigma_{i}^{z}\right)\right]}\ , (9)

with BB and CC indicating two of the three sublattices of the triangular lattice, along with an additional three-body contribution

T3​body​(𝝈)=exp⁡(i​β8​∑⟨i,j,k⟩γi​j​k​σiz​σjz​σkz),{T_{3\text{body}}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})=\exp\!\left(i\frac{\beta}{8}\sum_{\langle i,j,k\rangle}\gamma_{ijk}\sigma_{i}^{z}\sigma_{j}^{z}\sigma_{k}^{z}\right)}\ , (10)

leading to the sign prescription ΦHE​(𝝈)=ℜ⁡{T3​body​(𝝈)​Tclass​(𝝈)}{\Phi_{\mathrm{HE}}(\boldsymbol{\boldsymbol{\sigma}})=\Re\{T_{3\text{body}}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})T_{\text{class}}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})\}} [37, 8]. Here, β\beta is the only variational parameter, and the coefficients γi​j​k=0,±1\gamma_{ijk}=0,\pm 1 are chosen to preserve the symmetries of the classical Néel state [37, 8].

To quantify the agreement between sign structures, we follow Ref. [8] and define the mean sign overlap for a variational state Ψθ​(𝝈)\Psi_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) as

⟨s⟩=∑𝝈|Ψθ​(𝝈)|2​sgn​{ΦHE​(𝝈)​ℜ⁡[Ψθ​(𝝈)]}.\langle s\rangle=\sum_{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}|\Psi_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})|^{2}\,\mathrm{sgn}\!\left\{\Phi_{\text{HE}}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})\Re[\Psi_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})]\right\}. (11)

which can be stochastically estimated by sampling from |Ψθ​(𝝈)|2|\Psi_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma})|^{2}. In our case, the use of the real part of Ψθ​(𝝈)\Psi_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\sigma}) is justified by the fact that the phase distribution is sharply peaked around 00 and π\pi for the optimized states (see Section V.4). In Fig. 4a, we show the mean sign overlap between the ViT and the Huse–Elser state as a function of β\beta. Moreover, for L=6L=6 we also compare with the exact ground state; the ViT achieves a nearly perfect sign overlap, ⟨s⟩=0.99999707\langle s\rangle=0.99999707, confirming that the architecture can represent the correct sign structure at small sizes. While for L=6L=6 the Huse–Elser sign rule matches the exact signs well (for β≈0.27\beta\approx 0.27, ⟨s⟩≈0.96\langle s\rangle\approx 0.96) [7], the agreement deteriorates rapidly as the system grows. In Fig. 4b , we measure the mean sign overlap as a function of the number of sites L2L^{2}; for each size, we select the optimal β\beta for which the overlap is maximum. The overlap decays exponentially with the system size. The learned sign structure, therefore, differs markedly from both classical and the prescription proposed by Huse and Elser [37], indicating that sign information not captured by extended local prescriptions becomes increasingly important at large sizes. Interestingly, we observe distinct decay rates for the classical (β=0\beta=0) and Huse–Elser sign rules. This behavior suggests that systematically incorporating higher-order many-body contributions can further improve the overlap. At the same time, it indicates that the sign structure of the triangular lattice may be intrinsically non-local, such that no local unitary rotation in the computational basis can render the wave function positive definite [89].

IV J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg Square Lattice

The improvement provided by the Spatial Attention mechanism is not specific to triangular geometries or to Hamiltonians with only nearest-neighbor interactions. Because it relies solely on geometric information, the underlying physical principles are expected to remain effective across a broad class of models.

To demonstrate this generality, we consider the spin-1/21/2 J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model on a 20×2020\times 20 square lattice with periodic boundary conditions,

H^=J1​∑⟨i,j⟩𝑺^i⋅𝑺^j+J2​∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩𝑺^i⋅𝑺^j,\hat{H}=J_{1}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\!\langle i,j\rangle\!\rangle}\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{S}}_{j}, (12)

at the highly frustrated point J2/J1=0.5J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5, where various numerical studies have proposed the existence of a quantum spin liquid [58, 35]. The competing interactions in the strongly frustrated regime make the model a stringent benchmark for any variational Ansatz.

We compute the variational energy and obtain state-of-the-art results that surpass those achieved by a deep Residual Convolutional Neural Network augmented with a Lanczos step (ResNet2) from Ref. [10]. In Fig. 5, we report the energies obtained with increasing levels of symmetry restoration: no symmetry [−0.496375​(1)-0.496375(1)], translational symmetry [−0.496698​(1)-0.496698(1)], and full point-group (C4​vC_{4v}) symmetry [−0.496732​(1)-0.496732(1)]. A zero-variance extrapolation yields an energy of −0.49684​(1)-0.49684(1) (see Sec. V.3 for details) [5, 35]. The fully symmetric state attains a V-score of approximately 0.00190.0019 [102] and a relative error Δ​ε≈2.3×10−4\Delta\varepsilon\approx 2.3\times 10^{-4} with respect to the extrapolated value, demonstrating high accuracy even in this strongly frustrated regime.

Notably, the ViT Ansatz with translational symmetry alone already achieves an energy lower than both the ResNet2 result with one Lanczos step [5] and its zero-variance-extrapolated estimate reported in Ref. [10]. This further demonstrates that the proposed approach is not limited to the triangular-lattice Heisenberg model but extends naturally to other challenging quantum many-body Hamiltonians.

V Discussion

This work establishes a concrete route for extending variational methods to lattice sizes that were previously out of reach. We introduced the Spatial Attention mechanism, a minimal geometric inductive bias within the Vision Transformer architecture that fundamentally changes the practical regime accessible with Neural-Network Quantum States: it stabilizes large-scale optimization to the extent that controlled finite-size scaling becomes feasible even in frustrated two-dimensional systems. For the triangular-lattice Heisenberg antiferromagnet, this capability enables highly accurate estimates of thermodynamic-limit quantities, such as the ground-state energy, magnetization, and, in turn, experimentally measurable parameters such as spin-wave velocities and susceptibilities. It also clarifies a systematic source of variability in earlier estimates of the order parameter: less accurate variational states tend to overestimate magnetic order, leading to an apparent enhancement of magnetization.

Our results indicate that further extensions to even larger system sizes are primarily constrained by available computational resources rather than by conceptual or methodological limitations. Looking ahead, continued advances in hardware are expected to substantially increase the available computational capacity. Moreover, the inherently parallel structure of the Variational Monte Carlo framework makes the present approach well suited for efficient execution on large GPU clusters, enabling simulations to scale to larger lattice sizes at comparable accuracy without requiring fundamental modifications to the methodology. Promising future directions include improving optimization efficiency [82], enhancing sampling strategies [51], and reducing the computational cost of observable estimation through the use of mixed precision algorithms [83] and controlled approximations [47] that enable scaling to increasingly large systems.

We expect our variational approach to become a leading tool for the discovery and characterization of exotic phases of matter, such as quantum spin liquids [3, 77]. Beyond spin models, a natural extension is the use of this architecture as a backflow Ansatz for fermionic wave functions [47, 69, 70]. In this context, access to very large system sizes is essential to address long-standing and debated questions, such as the emergence of superconductivity in the two-dimensional Hubbard model [61, 104, 70], by enabling the direct evaluation of pairing correlation functions at increasingly large distances. Finally, the bias we introduce is entirely Hamiltonian-agnostic, providing a flexible foundation for future developments that extend variational simulations to increasingly complex Hamiltonians, well beyond the models considered here.

Methods

V.1 Literature Survey of Magnetization Estimates

In this Section, we compile reference values for the ground-state magnetization in the thermodynamic limit as reported in the literature using a variety of numerical and analytical methods. These estimates are summarized in Table 2 and ordered from larger to smaller magnetization. Notably, our result yields the smallest magnetization among all values currently available in the literature. Moreover, among approaches based on finite-size calculations, our study is performed on the largest cluster size considered to date.

V.2 Architecture and Optimization Details

The Vision Transformer architecture used in this work comprises h=12h=12 attention heads, nl=8n_{l}=8 layers, and an embedding dimension of d=72d=72, resulting in approximately P≈4.5×105P\approx 4.5\times 10^{5} trainable parameters for different system sizes, from L=18L=18 to L=42L=42. The input spin configuration 𝝈\boldsymbol{\sigma} is divided into nn non-overlapping patches of size b×bb\times b [96], each embedded into ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} through a learnable linear transformation, producing the sequence 𝒙i\boldsymbol{x}_{i} with i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n, where n=L2/b2n=L^{2}/b^{2}. In particular, we set b=3b=3 for the triangular lattice, which is compatible with the Néel 120∘120^{\circ} antiferromagnetic order and b=4b=4 for the square lattice (see Section IV). A detailed description of the role of the different hyperparameters of the architecture is provided in Ref. [96]. We take the attention weights to be translationally invariant across patches and enforce all remaining lattice symmetries, including translations within patches, rotations, and reflections (C6​vC_{6v} group for the triangular lattice and C4​vC_{4v} for the square lattice) through a projector operator in the trivial representation sector [59]. The only modification to the standard architecture presented in Ref. [96] is the inclusion of the Spatial Attention mechanism, where the variational parameter controlling the characteristic correlation range was initialized to γ=3\gamma=3 for all the heads and layers [see Eq. 1]. Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) optimizations employing M=214M=2^{14} samples for the stochastic estimates were carried out using SR [84] with the linear algebra trick being in the regime P≫MP\gg M [10, 66] enhanced with SPRING [27]. The optimization proceeded in three stages: 50005000 steps without symmetry summation, followed by 500500 steps including translational symmetries, and a final 100100 steps with both rotational and reflection symmetries restored. The initial learning rate was set to η=5×10−3\eta=5\times 10^{-3} and gradually decreased during training.

V.3 Energy-Variance Extrapolations

The eigenstates of a finite-size Hamiltonian can be classified according to the symmetry quantum numbers of the system. Although neural-network wave functions are universal approximators in the limit of sufficiently many parameters and can, in principle, represent any eigenstate of a given Hamiltonian, stochastic optimization does not automatically enforce these symmetries. As a result, the optimized variational state typically does not exactly satisfy the symmetry constraints.

Symmetry restoration can be performed a posteriori through quantum-number projection [59, 53]. This procedure not only enforces the exact symmetries of the Hamiltonian but also systematically improves the variational state, lowering the energy and reducing the variance. We can use this sequence of symmetry-projected states to perform a controlled variance extrapolation. Indeed, for a systematically improved sequence of states, it is easy to prove that εθ≈ε0+const×σθ2{\varepsilon_{\theta}\approx\varepsilon_{0}+\mathrm{const}\times\sigma_{\theta}^{2}}, where εθ=⟨Ψθ|H^|Ψθ⟩/L2{\varepsilon_{\theta}={\langle\Psi_{\theta}|\hat{H}|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle}/L^{2}} and σθ2=[⟨Ψθ|H^2|Ψθ⟩−⟨Ψθ|H^|Ψθ⟩2]/L2{\sigma_{\theta}^{2}=[{\langle\Psi_{\theta}|\hat{H}^{2}|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle-\langle\Psi_{\theta}|\hat{H}|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle^{2}}]/{L^{2}}} are the energy and variance per site of the normalized state |Ψθ⟩|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle [35, 5]. The exact energy per site ε0\varepsilon_{0} can therefore be obtained by fitting εθ\varepsilon_{\theta} as a function of σθ2\sigma_{\theta}^{2}.

For the Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice, the sequence of improved states consists of three levels of symmetry restoration: the unprojected state, the state projected onto translational symmetry, and the state projected onto the full point-group symmetry (C6​vC_{6v} group). As shown in Fig. 6, the accuracy of the wave function improves systematically across this sequence, enabling a reliable zero-variance extrapolation for each system size from L=18L=18 to L=42L=42. We further emphasize that the variance per site remains remarkably stable as the system size increases, indicating that the variational Ansatz is size consistent (as discussed also in Section III.1).

V.4 Distribution of Phases Amplitudes

Hamiltonians that respect time-reversal symmetry admit ground states that can be chosen to be real in the computational basis; equivalently, their many-body amplitudes carry phases restricted to 00 or π\pi, up to an overall global phase. Nonetheless, we work with complex-valued variational wavefunctions, as representing the sign structure in the complex plane substantially simplifies the optimization. However, we expect the optimized state to recover its real-valued character when converged [94].

In Fig. 7 we report the cumulative distribution function of the phases of the neural-network amplitudes associated with configurations sampled from the optimized variational state. The comparison across system sizes, from L=18L=18 up to L=42L=42, shows that the phase distribution remains sharply concentrated around 00 and π\pi. While the width of these peaks increases mildly with system size, the overall distribution for L=42L=42 remains strongly bimodal and extremely narrow, indicating that the optimized wavefunction is, to an excellent approximation, real-valued (see Inset of Fig. 7).

V.5 Comparison of Standard and Spatial Factored Attention at initialization

In Fig. 8, we compare the attention weights αi​j\alpha_{ij} at initialization, which determine the contribution of each patch to the updated representation of the central patch (marked by a red cross), for both the Factored attention mechanism [65] and the spatially weighted variant introduced in this work. In the standard mechanism (see Fig. 8a), the attention weights αi​j\alpha_{ij} show no spatial structure: all patches contribute with comparable strength. Such unstructured long-range parameters become increasingly challenging to optimize on large lattices. By contrast, with Spatial Attention (see Fig. 8b), the exponential kernel in Eq. 1 modulates the attention weights so that nearby patches receive systematically larger weights, while distant contributions are suppressed according to the learnable length scale γ\gamma. This embeds the spatial structure of the lattice directly at the architectural level, stabilizing the optimization for large system sizes.

I Finite-Size Corrections in a Quantum Antiferromagnet

I.1 Notation

Given a two-dimensional lattice of L×LL\times L spins on a torus generated by primitive lattice vectors 𝒂1{\bm{a}}_{1} and 𝒂2{\bm{a}_{2}}, we view the torus as the unit cell of an infinite lattice with lattice vectors 𝑨1=L​𝒂1{\bm{A}}_{1}=L{\bm{a}}_{1} and 𝑨2=L​𝒂2{\bm{A}}_{2}=L{\bm{a}}_{2} and lattice points 𝑹=n1​𝑨1+n2​𝑨2\bm{R}=n_{1}\bm{A}_{1}+n_{2}\bm{A}_{2} with n1,n2∈ℤn_{1},n_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}. The supercell area is

V=|𝑨1×𝑨2|=L2​|𝒂1×𝒂2|V=|\bm{A}_{1}\times\bm{A}_{2}|=L^{2}|\bm{a}_{1}\times\bm{a}_{2}| (1)

The corresponding reciprocal lattice vectors are defined as

𝑩1=2​πV​(𝑨2×𝒛^)𝑩2=2​πV​(𝒛^×𝑨1),\bm{B}_{1}=\frac{2\pi}{V}\,(\bm{A}_{2}\times\hat{\bm{z}})\qquad\bm{B}_{2}=\frac{2\pi}{V}\,(\hat{\bm{z}}\times\bm{A}_{1})\ , (2)

and satisfy 𝑨i⋅𝑩j=2​π​δi​j\bm{A}_{i}\cdot\bm{B}_{j}=2\pi\,\delta_{ij}. Allowed reciprocal vectors are therefore 𝑮=m1​𝑩1+m2​𝑩2\bm{G}=m_{1}\bm{B}_{1}+m_{2}\bm{B}_{2} with m1,m2∈ℤm_{1},m_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}. It is convenient to introduce primitive reciprocal vectors 𝒃i\bm{b}_{i} via 𝑩i=2​πL​𝒃i\bm{B}_{i}=\tfrac{2\pi}{L}\,\bm{b}_{i} such that 𝒂i⋅𝒃j=δi​j\bm{a}_{i}\cdot\bm{b}_{j}=\delta_{ij}. Then the norm of 𝑮\bm{G} can be written as

|𝑮|=2​πL​|𝒎|g|𝒎|g=𝒎T​g​𝒎,|\bm{G}|=\frac{2\pi}{L}\,|\bm{m}|_{g}\qquad|\bm{m}|_{g}=\sqrt{\bm{m}^{T}g\,\bm{m}}\ , (3)

where the metric tensor in reciprocal space is defined by gi​j=𝒃i⋅𝒃jg_{ij}=\bm{b}_{i}\cdot\bm{b}_{j}. The reciprocal-cell area satisfies

detg=|𝐛1×𝐛2|=1|𝐚1×𝐚2|,\sqrt{\det g}=|\mathbf{b}_{1}\times\mathbf{b}_{2}|=\frac{1}{|\mathbf{a}_{1}\times\mathbf{a}_{2}|}\ , (4)

so that eq. 1 can equivalently be written as V=L2/detgV=L^{2}/\sqrt{\det g}.

I.2 Ground-State Energy

In this section we extract the leading finite-size correction to the ground-state energy of a two-dimensional quantum antiferromagnet on a torus. In the continuum limit, the ground-state energy density at T=0T=0 for the triangular antiferromagnet is

e0=(∑ℓ=13cℓ2)​∫|𝐤|<Λd2​k4​π2​|𝐤|,e_{0}=\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\frac{c_{\ell}}{2}\right)\int_{|{\mathbf{k}}|<\Lambda}\frac{d^{2}k}{4\pi^{2}}|{\mathbf{k}}|\ , (5)

which depends on the ultraviolet cutoff Λ\Lambda. Following Ref. [22], we compute the finite-size corrections, which are independent of the cutoff. By dimensional analysis and scaling, the energy on a torus of volume V∝L2V\propto L^{2} admits the scaling form

EL2=e0+(∑ℓ=13cℓ2)​𝒞1L3+….\frac{E}{L^{2}}=e_{0}+\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\frac{c_{\ell}}{2}\right)\frac{\mathcal{C}_{1}}{L^{3}}+\dots\ . (6)

Here e0e_{0} depends on Λ\Lambda and is non-universal, whereas 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} is universal: it depends only on the modular parameter of the torus and is independent of the underlying lattice on which the spins sit.

In the discrete setting, the energy per unit volume can be expressed (after applying the Poisson summation formula) as

EV=(∑ℓ=13cℓ2)​1V​∑𝑮|𝑮|=(∑ℓ=13cℓ2)​∫ℝ2d2​k4​π2​∑𝑹ei​𝐤⋅𝑹​|𝐤|.\frac{E}{V}=\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\frac{c_{\ell}}{2}\right)\frac{1}{V}\sum_{{\bm{G}}}|{\bm{G}}|=\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\frac{c_{\ell}}{2}\right)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\frac{d^{2}k}{4\pi^{2}}\sum_{{\bm{R}}}e^{i{\mathbf{k}}\cdot{\bm{R}}}|{\mathbf{k}}|\ . (7)

Performing the Fourier transform of |𝐤||{\mathbf{k}}| and exploiting eq. 4, one obtains:

EL2=e0−1detg​(∑ℓ=13cℓ2)​∑𝑹≠𝟎12​π​|𝑹|3.\frac{E}{L^{2}}=e_{0}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{\det g}}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\frac{c_{\ell}}{2}\right)\sum_{{\bm{R}}\neq{\bm{0}}}\frac{1}{2\pi|{\bm{R}}|^{3}}\ . (8)

For the triangular lattice we choose 𝒂1=(1,0)\bm{a}_{1}=(1,0) and 𝒂2=(−12,32)\bm{a}_{2}=(-\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}). Then |𝑹|3=L3​(n12+n22−n1​n2)3/2|\bm{R}|^{3}=L^{3}\,(n_{1}^{2}+n_{2}^{2}-n_{1}n_{2})^{3/2} and we find

EL2=e0−(∑ℓ=13cℓ2)​[S△2​π​detg]​1L3,\frac{E}{L^{2}}=e_{0}-\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\frac{c_{\ell}}{2}\right)\left[\frac{S_{\triangle}}{2\pi\sqrt{\det g}}\right]\frac{1}{L^{3}}\ , (9)

where we have defined S△=∑(n1,n2)≠𝟎(n12+n22−n1n2)−3/2S_{\triangle}=\sum_{{(n_{1},n_{2})}\neq{\bm{0}}}(n_{1}^{2}+n_{2}^{2}-n_{1}n_{2})^{-3/2}. The last expression is of the form of eq. 6 with 𝒞1=−S△/(2πdetg)\mathcal{C}_{1}=-S_{\triangle}/(2\pi\sqrt{\det g}) where S△=6​ζ​(32)​L​(χ−3,32)=11.03417573S_{\triangle}=6\,\zeta\!\left(\tfrac{3}{2}\right)\,L\!\left(\chi_{-3},\tfrac{3}{2}\right)=11.03417573. Here, ζ⁡(⋅)\zeta(\cdot) is the Riemann zeta function and L⁡(χ−3,⋅)L(\chi_{-3},\cdot) is the Dirichlet LL-function associated with the Dirichlet character χ−3\chi_{-3} [6]. Finally, we obtain

𝒞1=−S△2​π​detg=−1.52086497.\boxed{\mathcal{C}_{1}=-\frac{S_{\triangle}}{2\pi\sqrt{\det g}}=-1.52086497}\ . (10)

The analogous calculation can be performed for the square lattice with 𝒂1=(1,0)\bm{a}_{1}=(1,0) and 𝒂2=(0,1)\bm{a}_{2}=(0,1), velocities c1=c2=cc_{1}=c_{2}=c, and detg=1\sqrt{\det g}=1. In this case [6]

S□=∑(n1,n2)≠𝟎1(n12+n22)3/2=4​ζ​(32)​β​(32)=9.03362168,S_{\square}=\sum_{(n_{1},n_{2})\neq\bm{0}}\frac{1}{(n_{1}^{2}+n_{2}^{2})^{3/2}}=4\,\zeta\!\left(\tfrac{3}{2}\right)\,\beta\!\left(\tfrac{3}{2}\right)=9.03362168\ , (11)

where β⁡(⋅)\beta(\cdot) is the Dirichlet beta function. We obtain 𝒞1=−S□/(2π)=−1.437745\mathcal{C}_{1}=-S_{\square}/(2\pi)=-1.437745, in agreement with Refs. [22, 73, 76].

I.3 Ground-State Magnetization

In this section we determine the leading finite-size correction to the ground-state magnetization of a two-dimensional quantum antiferromagnet on a torus. As stated in the main text, the magnetization on the triangular lattice is characterized by two orthogonal unit vectors 𝒏1\bm{n}_{1} and 𝒏2\bm{n}_{2}, which are related to zαz_{\alpha} by

(n1)a+i​(n2)a=zγ​εγ​α​σα​βa​zβ,(n_{1})^{a}+i\,(n_{2})^{a}=z_{\gamma}\,\varepsilon_{\gamma\alpha}\,\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\beta}\,z_{\beta}, (12)

We solve the constraint ∑α|zα|2=1\sum_{\alpha}|z_{\alpha}|^{2}=1 by parametrizing

z1=1−π12−π22−π32+i​π1,z2=π2+i​π3,\displaystyle z_{1}=\sqrt{1-\pi_{1}^{2}-\pi_{2}^{2}-\pi_{3}^{2}}+i\pi_{1},\qquad z_{2}=\pi_{2}+i\pi_{3}, (13)

where πℓ\pi_{\ell} are three real fields (ℓ=1,2,3\ell=1,2,3). To second order in πℓ\pi_{\ell}, the relation in eq. 12 implies

𝒏1=(1−2​(π12+π22)−2​π1−2​π2​π3−2​π2+2​π1​π3)+⋯,𝒏2=(2​π1−2​π2​π31−2​(π12+π32)−2​π3−2​π1​π2)+⋯.\bm{n}_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}1-2\left(\pi_{1}^{2}+\pi_{2}^{2}\right)\\ -2\pi_{1}-2\pi_{2}\pi_{3}\\ -2\pi_{2}+2\pi_{1}\pi_{3}\end{pmatrix}+\cdots,\qquad\bm{n}_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}2\pi_{1}-2\pi_{2}\pi_{3}\\ 1-2\left(\pi_{1}^{2}+\pi_{3}^{2}\right)\\ -2\pi_{3}-2\pi_{1}\pi_{2}\end{pmatrix}+\cdots. (14)

From this parametrization, and the action for πℓ\pi_{\ell} in the main text, we find that

c1=c∥,c2=c3=c⟂,c_{1}=c_{\parallel},\qquad c_{2}=c_{3}=c_{\perp}, (15)

as π1\pi_{1} is the in-plane mode, while π2,3\pi_{2,3} are the two out-of-plane modes.

We evaluate the structure factor on a torus of volume VV,

ℳ2ℳ02\displaystyle\frac{\mathcal{M}^{2}}{\mathcal{M}_{0}^{2}} =1V​∫d2​x​⟨𝒏1​(x,τ)⋅𝒏1​(0,τ)⟩\displaystyle=\frac{1}{V}\int d^{2}x\,\langle\bm{n}_{1}(x,\tau)\cdot\bm{n}_{1}(0,\tau)\rangle (16)
=1+4V​∑ℓ=12∫d​ω2​π​(1mℓ​ω2−∑𝑮1mℓ​(ω2+cℓ2​|𝑮|2))\displaystyle=1+\frac{4}{V}\sum_{\ell=1}^{2}\int\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}\left(\frac{1}{m_{\ell}\omega^{2}}-\sum_{\bm{G}}\frac{1}{m_{\ell}(\omega^{2}+c_{\ell}^{2}|\bm{G}|^{2})}\right) (17)
=1−2V​(∑ℓ=121mℓ​cℓ)​∑𝑮≠01|𝑮|.\displaystyle=1-\frac{2}{V}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{2}\frac{1}{m_{\ell}c_{\ell}}\right)\sum_{\bm{G}\neq 0}\frac{1}{|\bm{G}|}. (18)

Subtracting the infinite-volume answer, we have

ℳ2−ℳ02=−ℳ02​(∑ℓ=122mℓ​cℓ)​(1V​∑𝑮≠01|𝑮|−∫|𝒌|≤Λd2​k4​π2​1|𝒌|).\mathcal{M}^{2}-\mathcal{M}_{0}^{2}=-\mathcal{M}_{0}^{2}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{2}\frac{2}{m_{\ell}c_{\ell}}\right)\left(\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\bm{G}\neq 0}\frac{1}{|\bm{G}|}-\int_{|\bm{k}|\leq\Lambda}\frac{d^{2}k}{4\pi^{2}}\,\frac{1}{|\bm{k}|}\right). (19)

The limit Λ→+∞\Lambda\to+\infty should exist after the subtraction; in practice, one may introduce a smooth cutoff. This yields a result of the form

ℳ2​(L)=ℳ02+ℳ02​(∑ℓ=122mℓ​cℓ)​𝒞2L,\mathcal{M}^{2}(L)=\mathcal{M}_{0}^{2}+\mathcal{M}_{0}^{2}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{2}\frac{2}{m_{\ell}c_{\ell}}\right)\frac{\mathcal{C}_{2}}{L}\ , (20)

similar to eq. 6. Here 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} is a universal number which depends only on the modular parameter of the torus.

To extract 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} we evaluate the difference between the discrete reciprocal-lattice sum and the corresponding continuum integral in eq. 19. Each term diverges, but their difference is finite.

We use two complementary regularizations to validate the result. First, we introduce an exponential regulator 11 1 This is equivalent to a hard momentum cutoff Λ\Lambda in eq. 19, but it improves numerical convergence. and define

Δη​(L)≡1V​∑𝐆≠𝟎e−η​|𝐆||𝐆|−∫ℝ2d2​𝐤4​π2​e−η​|𝐤||𝐤|.\Delta_{\eta}(L)\equiv\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\mathbf{G}\neq\mathbf{0}}\frac{e^{-\eta\,|\mathbf{G}|}}{|\mathbf{G}|}-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\frac{d^{2}\mathbf{k}}{4\pi^{2}}\,\frac{e^{-\eta\,|\mathbf{k}|}}{|\mathbf{k}|}\ . (21)

The continuum integral can be evaluated explicitly using polar coordinates in 𝐤\mathbf{k}.

∫ℝ2d2​𝐤4​π2​e−η​|𝐤||𝐤|=12​π​η.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\frac{d^{2}\mathbf{k}}{4\pi^{2}}\,\frac{e^{-\eta\,|\mathbf{k}|}}{|\mathbf{k}|}=\frac{1}{2\pi\eta}\ . (22)

Introducing the dimensionless regulator ε≡(2​π​η)/L\varepsilon\equiv(2\pi\eta)/L and exploiting eq. 4 and eq. 3, we arrive at the following dimensionless expression:

Δε​(L)≡12​π​L​[detg​∑𝐦≠𝟎e−ε​|𝐦|g|𝐦|g−2​πε].\Delta_{\varepsilon}(L)\equiv\frac{1}{2\pi L}\left[\sqrt{\det g}\sum_{\mathbf{m}\neq\mathbf{0}}\frac{e^{-\varepsilon|\mathbf{m}|_{g}}}{|\mathbf{m}|_{g}}-\frac{2\pi}{\varepsilon}\right]\ . (23)

For the small-ε\varepsilon expansion we expect

∑𝐦≠𝟎e−ε​|𝐦|g|𝐦|g​∼ε→0​2​πε​detg+C+O⁡(ε).\sum_{\mathbf{m}\neq\mathbf{0}}\frac{e^{-\varepsilon|\mathbf{m}|_{g}}}{|\mathbf{m}|_{g}}\underset{\varepsilon\rightarrow 0}{\sim}\frac{2\pi}{\varepsilon\,\sqrt{\det g}}+C+O(\varepsilon)\ . (24)

Consequently, we can extract the finite part as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0:

Δε​(L)​∼ε→0​12​π​L​[detg​(2​πε​detg+C+O⁡(ε))−2​πε]=12​π​L​detg​C+O⁡(ε).\Delta_{\varepsilon}(L)\underset{\varepsilon\rightarrow 0}{\sim}\frac{1}{2\pi L}\left[\sqrt{\det g}\left(\frac{2\pi}{\varepsilon\,\sqrt{\det g}}+C+O(\varepsilon)\right)-\frac{2\pi}{\varepsilon}\right]=\frac{1}{2\pi L}\,\sqrt{\det g}\,C+O(\varepsilon)\ . (25)

In the end, the finite contribution can be rewritten as

𝒞2≡−detg​C2​π.\mathcal{C}_{2}\equiv-\frac{\sqrt{\det g}\ C}{2\pi}\ . (26)

The latter can be computed numerically by evaluating the difference between the discrete sum and the integral for several values of ε\varepsilon and then extrapolating to ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, yielding 𝒞2≈0.670583\mathcal{C}_{2}\approx 0.670583 (see fig. 1).

As an alternative approach, we use zeta-function regularization [32], which yields an analytic result. We start by defining the lattice sum appearing in the eq. 23

Zg=detg​∑𝒎≠𝟎1|𝒎|g=∑(m1,m2)≠𝟎1(m12+m22+m1​m2)1/2.Z_{g}=\sqrt{\det g}\sum_{\bm{m}\neq\bm{0}}\frac{1}{|\bm{m}|_{g}}=\sum_{(m_{1},m_{2})\neq\bm{0}}\frac{1}{(m_{1}^{2}+m_{2}^{2}+m_{1}m_{2})^{1/2}}\ . (27)

Here we used |𝒎|g=23​(m2+n2+m​n)1/2|\bm{m}|_{g}=\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}(m^{2}+n^{2}+mn)^{1/2} and detg=23\sqrt{\det g}=\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.

The series in eq. 27 is divergent. However, it can be defined by analytic continuation via the triangular-lattice Epstein zeta function [6],

Z△​(s)=∑(m1,m2)≠𝟎1(m12+m1​m2+m22)s,s∈ℂ,Re⁡(s)>1.Z_{\triangle}(s)=\sum_{(m_{1},m_{2})\neq\bm{0}}\frac{1}{\left(m_{1}^{2}+m_{1}m_{2}+m_{2}^{2}\right)^{s}}\ ,\qquad s\in\mathbb{C},\ \operatorname{Re}(s)>1\,. (28)

This function admits an analytic continuation and a functional equation.

One finds the factorization

ZΔ​(s)=6​ζ​(s)​L​(χ−3,s),Z_{\Delta}(s)=6\,\zeta(s)\,L(\chi_{-3},s)\ , (29)

where ζ⁡(⋅)\zeta(\cdot) is the Riemann zeta function and L⁡(χ−3,⋅)L(\chi_{-3},\cdot) is the Dirichlet LL-function associated with the Dirichlet character χ−3\chi_{-3} [6]. Notice that eq. 29 admits a meromorphic continuation to the complex plane with a single simple pole at s=1s=1. One finds by analytic continuation that, for s=1/2s=1/2

ZΔ​(12)=6​ζ​(12)​L​(χ−3,12)=−4.21342263613690689003.Z_{\Delta}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)=6\,\zeta\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)\,L\!\left(\chi_{-3},\tfrac{1}{2}\right)=-4.21342263613690689003\ . (30)

With this procedure we can directly extract the finite part of the series without subtracting divergent contribution [32] and obtaining

𝒞2=−Z△​(12)2​π=0.670587039.\boxed{\mathcal{C}_{2}=-\frac{Z_{\triangle}(\tfrac{1}{2})}{2\pi}=0.670587039}\ . (31)

Notice that the result obtained with the latter approach matches the one obtained with the exponential cutoff regularization (see fig. 1).

The analogous calculation can be performed for the square lattice defining

Z□​(s)=∑(m1,m2)≠𝟎1(m12+m22)s,Z_{\square}(s)=\sum_{{(m_{1},m_{2})}\neq{\bm{0}}}\frac{1}{(m_{1}^{2}+m_{2}^{2})^{s}}\ , (32)

which can be derived analytically as Z□​(s)=4​ζ​(s)​β​(s)Z_{\square}(s)=4\,\zeta\!\left(s\right)\,\beta\!\left(s\right), and evaluated at s=12s=\tfrac{1}{2} obtaining Z□​(12)=−3.900264920001{Z_{\square}(\tfrac{1}{2})=-3.900264920001} and consequently 𝒞2=−Z□(s)/(2π)=0.62074644{\mathcal{C}_{2}=-Z_{\square}(s)}/(2\pi)=0.62074644 in agreement with Refs. [73, 76].

II Numerical Results from Linear Spin-Wave Theory

We consider the spin-12\tfrac{1}{2} Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the triangular lattice. In this section we report the results obtained with linear spin wave theory following Ref. [14] and setting throughout S=12,J=1,a=1S=\tfrac{1}{2},J=1,a=1. The two independent spin-wave velocities are

c∥0=3​32​J​S​ac⟂0=3​32​2​J​S​a.c^{0}_{\parallel}=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}JSa\qquad c^{0}_{\perp}=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2\sqrt{2}}JSa\ . (33)

Including the 1/S1/S corrections, the renormalized velocities read

cSW∥=c∥0(1−0.1152​S)cSW⟂=c⟂0(1+0.0832​S).c_{\text{SW}\parallel}=c^{0}_{\parallel}\left(1-\frac{0.115}{2S}\right)\qquad c_{\text{SW}\perp}=c^{0}_{\perp}\left(1+\frac{0.083}{2S}\right)\ . (34)

For S=12S=\tfrac{1}{2} this gives

cSW∥=1.1496487235238424cSW⟂=0.9947990217878181.c_{\text{SW}\parallel}=1.1496487235238424\qquad c_{\text{SW}\perp}=0.9947990217878181\ . (35)

The uniform susceptibilities are given by

χSW⟂=29​3​J​a2(1−0.2852​S)χSW∥=29​3​J​a2(1−0.4492​S).\chi_{\text{SW}\perp}=\frac{2}{9\sqrt{3}Ja^{2}}\left(1-\frac{0.285}{2S}\right)\qquad\chi_{\text{SW}\parallel}=\frac{2}{9\sqrt{3}Ja^{2}}\left(1-\frac{0.449}{2S}\right)\ . (36)

For S=12S=\tfrac{1}{2} one finds

χSW∥=0.07069333296077418χSW⟂=0.09173454277124056.\chi_{\text{SW}\parallel}=0.07069333296077418\qquad\chi_{\text{SW}\perp}=0.09173454277124056\ . (37)

The corresponding masses entering the nonlinear σ\sigma-model are m1=4​χ∥m_{1}=4\chi_{\parallel}, m2=m3=4​χ⟂m_{2}=m_{3}=4\chi_{\perp} and using the relations c1=c∥c_{1}=c_{\parallel}, c2=c3=c⟂c_{2}=c_{3}=c_{\perp} the coefficient entering the finite-size correction to the ground-state energy is

c¯=c∥+2​c⟂=3.1392467670994786.\bar{c}=c_{\parallel}+2c_{\perp}=3.1392467670994786\ . (38)

Similarly, the coefficient controlling the finite-size scaling of the magnetization is given by

1c​χ¯SW=12​(1cSW∥χSW∥+1cSW⟂​χSW⟂)=11.631148207320964,\frac{1}{\overline{c\chi}_{\text{SW}}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{c_{\text{SW}\parallel}\chi_{\text{SW}\parallel}}+\frac{1}{c_{\text{SW}\perp}\chi_{\text{SW}\perp}}\right)=11.631148207320964\ , (39)

and as a result c​χ¯SW=0.08597603453{\overline{c\chi}_{\text{SW}}}=0.08597603453.
